safetyNote: Listed as edible by the German Society for Mycology and Swiss VAPKO, but often considered less palatable than other orange milkcaps because its latex or flesh can taste bitter. Eat only after reliable identification and suitable cooking; do not use taste as an identification test. Similar Lactarius species require checking the host tree, stem surface, gills and the changing colour of fresh latex together. If identification is uncertain, seek expert review and do not eat it.

sections.title: Orange cap that greens
sections.text: The cap is initially convex with an inrolled edge, then broadens and develops a central depression, usually about 5–12 cm across. It is carrot to brick orange, slippery when wet, with weak to sometimes clearer darker zones. Green patches commonly appear with age or after handling, at times even on young specimens. The mature margin may become wavy.

sections.title: Gills, stem and changing milk
sections.text: The crowded orange gills run a short distance down the stem and stain green when bruised. A fresh cut releases carrot-orange latex, often not abundant; it changes toward dark or wine red over roughly 10–30 minutes and may darken green later. The orange stem is relatively smooth and lacks the conspicuous sunken pits of Lactarius deliciosus; a paler band is often visible just under the gills. The stem may become hollow with age. The spore deposit is pale pinkish buff.

sections.title: Spruce association and comparisons
sections.text: European Lactarius deterrimus forms mycorrhizae chiefly with spruce (Picea), often in plantations or acidic conifer soil. It fruits mainly in late summer and autumn. The related Lactarius deliciosus grows with pine and more often has a clearly pitted stem; Lactarius salmonicolor is associated with fir and generally lacks the strong green staining. Host and appearance must both be checked because orange milkcaps are similar and older or dry specimens may yield little latex. North American records using the name L. deterrimus may refer to different taxa.

sections.title: Edibility and field caution
sections.text: The DGfM and VAPKO both include L. deterrimus on their edible mushroom lists. First Nature notes that even well-cooked specimens may retain a bitter flavour, so culinary assessments vary. A British Mycological Society key puts it among the orange-milk species and separates it from its fir and pine relatives by the spruce association. Keep a complete specimen and observe latex from a fresh cut over time; a single still image cannot show the colour reaction or establish edibility.

traits: Carrot to brick-orange cap, usually 5–12 cm, depressed with age and often blotched green
Cap slightly viscid when wet, with weak or variable concentric zoning
Crowded orange, shortly decurrent gills that stain green on injury
Orange latex changing to wine or dark red in roughly 10–30 minutes, then sometimes green
Orange smooth stem without conspicuous pits, often with a pale band near its top; hollowing with age
European collections chiefly mycorrhizal with spruce; pale pinkish-buff spore deposit
